summary: Exhaustive architectural review of adboost transport/multiplexer layer: find siblings of the TCP cancel-safety bug class + other correctness issues, adversarially verify each, synthesize
logs: Reviewing adboost transport+multiplexer layer across 6 correctness lenses, verifying each finding adversarially.
Found 13 candidate findings; 10 survived adversarial verification, 3 refuted.

synthesis.summary: The transport/multiplexer core is structurally fragile along one dominant axis: the TCP/async read and write paths lack a robustness guarantee the USB path already encodes, namely that a per-read/per-write timeout must never be observed mid-frame. The dominant recurring bug class is "non-cancel-safe partial I/O on a framed stream with no cross-call residual buffer" (a.k.a. cancel-safety / partial-read desync). adboost frames a byte stream (24-byte header + bounded payload) and multiplexes many logical sessions over one physical connection, so a single mid-frame desync is catastrophic: it doesn't drop one frame, it poisons the shared connection and tears down every session on it. The USB path is immune by accident of two unrelated properties (a persistent read_residual carried across calls, and nusb's atomic transfer cancellation), while the TCP path wraps non-cancel-safe tokio combinators (read_exact / write_all) in tokio::time::timeout with zero buffering, so a dropped future loses bytes that are already off the wire (read) or already on the wire (write). The reader loop's own doc correctly states a frame read must be atomic and that ReadTimeout means "nothing consumed" — but the TCP impl is the one transport that breaks both invariants, and the writer loop has no fatal-error path at all. This is the exact meta-pattern of the last several commits (split read/write halves, set TCP_NODELAY, unify read-timeout contract): each time, the async/TCP path was missing a guarantee USB already had. The architecture will keep generating this class of external-reporter bug until the framing/timeout invariant is enforced in ONE shared layer used by both transports rather than re-implemented (and mis-implemented) per transport. A secondary, independent class is "allocate/slice from an untrusted wire-supplied length" — the message transports standardized payload_len_within_bound(MAX_PAYLOAD), but the proxy sync commands and the sync-pull DONE-trailer decode never adopted it, yielding one guaranteed remote-triggerable panic and several unbounded allocations.

deduped.title: TCP read_message_with_timeout is not cancel-safe: a mid-frame reader-loop timeout drops already-read bytes and permanently desyncs the framed stream, tearing down every multiplexed session
deduped.lines: 108-120 (read_exact_timeout); 244-288 (read_message_with_timeout, header read at 253, payload read at 269)
deduped.scenario: This is the verified reference bug, consolidating four overlapping verified findings (read_exact partial-byte loss, the read-lock dimension, and the timeout-contract framing — all the same defect at the same site). read_exact_timeout does tokio::time::timeout(timeout, reader.read_exact(buf)). AsyncReadExt::read_exact is NOT cancel-safe: on elapse the future is dropped and bytes already moved off the socket into the call-local buf are lost; TcpTransport keeps no read_residual. read_message_with_timeout calls it twice with the SAME 1s reader-loop timeout (persistent.rs:1176): once for the 24-byte header, once for the data_length payload. Two concrete desync paths: (a) the payload read times out after pulling N-of-M payload bytes — those bytes are gone, ReadTimeout is returned, the reader loop classifies it benign (ReadStep::ReadTimeout => continue, persistent.rs:1013) and the next iteration reads its 24-byte header starting mid-payload; (b) the header read completes but the payload-phase read times out, so the neutral ReadTimeout is returned AFTER the header was already consumed off the wire while the payload is still pending — same misalignment. Either way the next header decode hits an illegal command word -> ADBTransportMessageHeader::try_from -> RustADBError::ConversionError, which the reader loop treats as FATAL (only InvalidIntegrity is recoverable, persistent.rs:1039) -> break -> the whole multiplexed connection is torn down, killing every session. Confirmed: tcp_transport.rs has no read_residual / BufReader / FramedRead; USB is immune via Connection.read_residual carried across calls + nusb atomic transfer cancellation.
deduped.suggestedFix: Give the TCP read path the cross-call durability USB has, enforcing one invariant: the neutral ReadTimeout may ONLY be returned when ZERO bytes of the current frame have been consumed. Either (a) add a per-connection read_residual/partial-fill buffer and a manual fill loop that preserves bytes already read and resumes on the next call (mirroring usb_transport read_exact + fill_and_carry), or (b) apply the idle timeout only to the FIRST byte of a frame and, once any frame byte is consumed, read the rest of the frame to completion with no mid-frame cancellation (long/disconnect-only deadline). Use a single deadline across header+payload (timeout_at) rather than re-arming the same per-call timeout twice.

deduped.title: TCP write_message_with_timeout leaves a partially-written frame on the wire on timeout and the writer_loop appends the next frame to the truncation, permanently desyncing the host->device stream
deduped.scenario: Write-side sibling of the read bug, same root cause (non-cancel-safe I/O wrapped in tokio::time::timeout, no atomicity guarantee). write_all_timeout wraps writer.write_all(data) + flush() in tokio::time::timeout. AsyncWriteExt::write_all is NOT cancel-safe: it advances an internal cursor across poll_write calls handing bytes to the kernel send buffer; when the 2s DEFAULT_WRITE_TIMEOUT fires under genuine TCP backpressure (full kernel buffer / stalled peer), the already-flushed prefix is delivered to adbd and cannot be recalled, the tail is abandoned -> a truncated ADB frame on the wire. write_message_with_timeout calls it twice (header then payload), so the split can land inside the 24-byte header, between header and payload, or mid-payload. Worse, the writer_loop has NO fatal classification: a FireForget write error only tracing::warn!s and continues; a WithAck error is forwarded over the oneshot and the loop continues. The loop then recv()s the NEXT OutboundFrame and writes it onto the SAME socket directly after the truncation -> permanent host->device frame desync for every session on the connection. (The WithAck path does call shared.mark_closed() via poll_inflight_write, but that retires only the one issuing session; FireForget OKAY/CLSE/OPEN and other live sessions keep writing onto the corrupted stream.) The IOError(TimedOut) encoding is correct for the read-only trait contract and is not the defect; the partial-write-then-continue is.
deduped.suggestedFix: A partially-written ADB frame is unrecoverable for the framed peer, so a mid-frame write timeout must be connection-fatal, not a per-frame soft error. Two parts: (1) in the transport, once any byte of a frame has been written, a subsequent timeout must poison the write half (shut it down / mark dead) instead of returning a recoverable-looking error; (2) in persistent.rs::writer_loop, a fatal write failure must break the loop and tear the connection down (matching the reader's fatal handling), since after a partial write alignment with the device is gone. Alternatively apply timeouts only at frame boundaries (write each frame atomically) and rely on socket-level write timeouts.

deduped.title: USB read_exact loses partially-read frame bytes when a later transfer in a multi-transfer field times out, then returns the benign ReadTimeout -> stream desync
deduped.scenario: Same invariant violation as the TCP bug, narrower trigger. read_exact loops while offset < out.len(), issuing one bulk IN transfer per iteration because a single frame field can span multiple transfers (a short packet ends a transfer early; confirmed by test fill_and_carry_short_packet_partial_fill, which leaves residual empty). nusb cancellation is atomic for ONE transfer, but if an EARLIER transfer in the field succeeded (copy_len bytes written into the call-local out, offset advanced) and a LATER transfer times out, transfer_with_timeout returns Cancelled -> map_transfer_status -> RustADBError::ReadTimeout, propagated by `?`. The bytes already in out[..offset] are dropped (out is call-local; fill_and_carry only stashes OVER-read overshoot into residual, never bytes already written into dst), while their remainder is still on the wire. classify_read_result maps ReadTimeout -> ReadStep::ReadTimeout -> reader loop continues and restarts a fresh 24-byte header read at the field remainder -> desync, exactly like TCP. The 'USB is immune' assumption holds only for a single transfer; it breaks for any payload larger than one aligned transfer under a mid-field stall crossing the 1s deadline.
deduped.suggestedFix: Make read_exact frame-atomic against a mid-field timeout the same way over-read is carried: on a ReadTimeout with offset>0, stash the partially-filled out[..offset] into a per-connection partial-field carry so the next call resumes instead of restarting a header read; OR only honor the timeout at a frame boundary (offset==0 AND empty residual) and once any byte of a frame is consumed keep reading to field completion ignoring the per-read deadline. Same invariant as the TCP fix: ReadTimeout only when zero frame bytes consumed.

deduped.title: recv_file slices payload[len-8..len-4] with no length guard -> remote-triggerable panic on an empty/short device WRTE frame
deduped.scenario: recv_file (sync pull, reached via pull() over both USB and TCP core transports -> commands/pull.rs:61) unconditionally slices the DONE trailer out of the raw device payload: payload[(payload.len()-8)..(payload.len()-4)]. The transport accepts any data_length in 0..=MAX_PAYLOAD (0 is explicitly allowed). For an EMPTY (0-byte) payload — a fully valid frame — the inner `while rdr.position() != payload.len()` loop is skipped and execution falls through to the slice; payload.len()-8 underflows usize (wraps to ~1.8e19) and the slice index is out of bounds, panicking the task. This is remote-controlled by a hostile or buggy device sending an empty WRTE. (Correction to the original report: 1..=7-byte payloads most likely return a structured EOF error from read_u32's `?` rather than panic; the guaranteed panic is the empty-payload path.)
deduped.suggestedFix: Guard the length before slicing: `if payload.len() < 8 { return Err(RustADBError::ConversionError); }` (or treat a short trailer as 'not DONE, keep looping'). Use checked subtraction / payload.get(payload.len()-8..payload.len()-4) and map None to a structured error so a short/empty device frame cannot panic the process.

deduped.title: writer_loop never tears down on a persistently failing write half; is_alive() ignores the writer, so a half-open connection is reported alive and reused while inbound credit (FireForget OKAY) is silently lost
deduped.scenario: writer_loop drains the outbound queue forever with no fatal classification: a FireForget write error is logged-and-dropped and the loop continues; a WithAck error is forwarded to the one caller and the loop continues. is_alive() consults only reader_handle, so when the write direction breaks while the read direction merely idles (only ReadTimeout -> continue), the connection reports is_alive()=true and default_backend reuses it. The inbound flow-control crediting OKAY is enqueued FireForget, so on a half-open write half those credits are silently lost: the peer stalls for lack of credit, the reader sees only idle timeouts, nothing ever breaks -> a quiet deadlock with no teardown. (Correction to the original report: WRTE data writes are NOT silent — the WithAck error is surfaced to the application and calls shared.mark_closed(), retiring that one session. The real residual defect is the missing connection-level teardown, is_alive ignoring writer_handle, and silent FireForget credit loss.)
deduped.suggestedFix: Classify write errors like the reader does: on a transport-fatal write failure (BrokenPipe/NotConnected, non-timeout nusb error) signal teardown — set conn_closed / drop the writer so subsequent enqueues fail fast, and/or abort the reader — instead of looping forever. At minimum have is_alive() also reflect writer_handle.is_finished() so a dead writer is observable to connection-reuse logic.

deduped.title: Proxy framebuffer allocates vec![0u8; framebuffer_info.size] from an unbounded device u32 (no payload_len_within_bound analogue)
deduped.scenario: framebuffer_inner reads the FrameBufferInfoV1/V2 struct off the connection then does vec![0u8; framebuffer_info.size as usize] where size is a device-controlled u32 (up to ~4 GiB). The try_into() only fails on 32-bit usize; on 64-bit it always succeeds, so there is no upper bound. A garbled/malicious framebuffer header drives one immediate multi-GiB allocation (OOM/abort) before any data is read. The message-transport read paths gate every payload alloc behind payload_len_within_bound(MAX_PAYLOAD); the message-device framebuffer equivalent grows a Vec frame-by-frame; this proxy path is the one that never adopted the bound. Same meta-pattern (a path missing a guarantee the rest of the codebase standardized) but a different bug class from the cancel-safety desync.
deduped.suggestedFix: Bound framebuffer_info.size against a sane maximum (width*height*4 via checked_mul, or a fixed cap) before allocating, mirroring payload_len_within_bound; reject oversize with ADBRequestFailed instead of allocating blindly.

deduped.title: Proxy LIST/RECV allocate vec![0u8; len] from an unbounded LE u32 read off the wire
deduped.scenario: In the LIST/DENT path, name_len = connection.read_u32_le() is a raw device-supplied u32 used directly as vec![0u8; name_len as usize] with no upper bound, before any read. Same pattern in recv.rs FAIL branch (error_msg length). A malicious/corrupt device response can request ~4 GiB per entry. Lower severity: the channel is proxy->local adb server (127.0.0.1:5037), the threat actor is a relayed device, vec![0;n] aborts rather than corrupts, and the following read_exact will EOF/fail. Still an alloc-from-wire DoS gap missing the MAX_PAYLOAD-style guard. (recv.rs DATA branch is safe — it reads in 65535-byte chunks.)
deduped.suggestedFix: Clamp these wire lengths to a reasonable maximum (filename / error-string sized, e.g. a few KiB, or at most MAX_PAYLOAD) before allocating, or read incrementally into a bounded buffer rather than pre-sizing from the untrusted length.

architecturalRecommendations: Introduce ONE shared cancel-safe, residual-buffered framed-read layer used by BOTH usb_transport and tcp_transport (and the proxy where it speaks the frame protocol), instead of each transport re-implementing read_exact_timeout. The layer owns a persistent read buffer and enforces a single invariant: a frame read either completes fully or returns ReadTimeout having consumed ZERO bytes of the current frame; partial progress is always retained across calls. This collapses ranks 1 and 3 into one correct implementation and removes the structural reason USB and TCP keep diverging.

Make the timeout-contract invariant executable, not just documented. Add transport contract tests that run against EVERY ADBMessageTransport impl (TCP, USB, proxy, emulator) via a scriptable byte source that can: (a) deliver a frame in fragments straddling the deadline, (b) deliver a header then stall before the payload, (c) deliver a short packet mid-field (USB), (d) stall mid-write under backpressure. Assert: ReadTimeout is only ever observed at a frame boundary, and a subsequent read still decodes the next frame correctly (no desync). These tests would have caught ranks 1, 2, and 3 and will catch the next transport added.

Treat a mid-frame WRITE timeout as connection-fatal at a shared layer and unify writer teardown. Give the writer the same fatal/recoverable classification the reader has, and make a partial write poison the connection rather than letting writer_loop append the next frame to a truncation. Have is_alive() reflect BOTH reader_handle and writer_handle so a half-open connection is never handed back out for reuse (fixes ranks 2 and 5).

Standardize 'allocate/index from a wire-supplied length' through one bounded helper. payload_len_within_bound(MAX_PAYLOAD) already exists for the message transports; extend the same discipline (a checked, capped length -> Result, never a bare `as usize` + vec!/slice) to the proxy sync commands and the sync-pull trailer decode. Add a clippy/lint or a small wrapper type (BoundedWireLen) so a raw read_u32 feeding an allocation or a slice index is a reviewable, greppable pattern. This addresses ranks 4, 6, and 7 as a class and stops the next proxy command from re-introducing it.

Add a single decode/invariant-checking layer at the frame boundary that converts the dangerous slice in recv_file (and similar trailer/offset arithmetic) into checked_sub / slice::get returning structured errors, so no wire-controlled length can ever underflow a usize or index out of bounds. Pair with a fuzz/property test that feeds arbitrary-length (including 0-byte) payloads through the sync-pull and proxy decoders to assert no panic path remains.

Codify the meta-pattern as a review checklist tied to the project rule 'one bug = one task = one commit': whenever the USB path has a robustness property (residual buffering, atomic cancellation, fatal-error teardown), require the TCP/async/proxy path to demonstrate the equivalent guarantee or a shared abstraction. The recurring external-reporter bugs are all 'the async path is missing a guarantee USB already has' — making that asymmetry a first-class review gate is cheaper than catching each instance after a report.

confirmed.title: read_exact_timeout drops partially-read bytes on timeout, permanently desyncing the TCP frame stream (the verified root-cause bug)
confirmed.scenario: read_message_with_timeout (lines 252-269) calls read_exact_timeout once for the 24-byte header and once for the data_length payload, with the reader loop's 1s timeout. AsyncReadExt::read_exact is NOT cancel-safe: when tokio::time::timeout fires, the read_exact future is dropped and any bytes already moved into `buf` are lost. If the timeout crosses a partial read (e.g. 10 of 24 header bytes, or part of a payload arrived), those bytes are gone but remain consumed-from-the-OS-buffer-perspective only for the dropped portion — the stream is now misaligned. The next read_message_with_timeout reads from the middle of the previous frame: the header decode (ADBTransportMessageHeader::try_from) hits an illegal command word -> RustADBError::ConversionError. The persistent reader (persistent.rs:1018-1044) classifies ConversionError as FATAL (only InvalidIntegrity is treated as frame-aligned/recoverable), so the whole multiplexed connection is torn down. USB is immune because Connection.read_residual carries over-read bytes across calls AND nusb timeout is an atomic transfer cancellation.
confirmed.suggestedFix: Give TcpTransport the same robustness guarantee USB already has: persist partial-read progress across calls. Either (a) keep a per-connection read_residual/partial-fill buffer and a manual fill loop (mirroring usb_transport::read_exact), polling read() in a loop and only returning ReadTimeout when ZERO bytes have been read since the last complete frame boundary; or (b) wrap the whole socket in a tokio_util FramedRead/length-buffered reader whose internal buffer survives a dropped poll. The invariant must be: a timeout may only be reported at a frame boundary (0 bytes of the current frame consumed); never mid-frame.
confirmed.verifierReasoning: Confirmed against actual code. tcp_transport.rs:108-120 read_exact_timeout wraps `reader.read_exact(buf)` in `tokio::time::timeout`; on elapse it drops the read_exact future and returns ReadTimeout. tokio's AsyncReadExt::read_exact is explicitly documented as NOT cancel-safe: bytes already moved into `buf` before cancellation are lost. read_message_with_timeout (lines 252-269) calls this once for the 24-byte header and once for the data_length payload with the reader loop's timeout, and there is NO mitigation: grep confirms tcp_transport.rs has no read_residual, no BufReader, no FramedRead — the only buffering machinery is the per-call stack `buf`. By contrast usb_transport.rs DOES carry a read_residual: Vec<u8> (line 66) across calls and nusb cancellation is atomic, so USB is immune — exactly as the finding states. The downstream classification is verified: an unknown command word in the misread header drives MessageCommand::try_from -> RustADBError::ConversionError (adb_transport_message.rs:130-131 in decode()), and the persistent reader (persistent.rs:1018-1044) treats only InvalidIntegrity as recoverable, classifying ConversionError as FATAL and breaking the loop, tearing down the whole multiplexed connection. The full failure chain (mid-frame timeout -> lost bytes -> stream desync -> bogus header -> ConversionError -> fatal teardown) holds end-to-end given the actual code. This is the verified root-cause bug. Minor wording garble in the finding's parenthetical about OS-buffer accounting does not affect the substantive, correct claim.

confirmed.title: write_all_timeout leaves a partially-written frame on the wire on timeout, desyncing the PEER's frame decoder (write-side sibling of the read bug)
confirmed.scenario: write_message_with_timeout (lines 290-308) calls write_all_timeout twice: once for the 24-byte header, once for the payload. write_all is not cancel-safe under cancellation: tokio::time::timeout dropping the inner future after write_all has flushed only part of the buffer leaves a truncated frame (or a header with no/partial payload) on the TCP socket — already delivered to the peer (adbd), which reads a framed stream. This is the exact inverse of the read desync: the device's frame decoder now reads a short/garbled frame and the rest of OUR next frame's bytes get appended to the truncation, permanently desyncing the device->host direction. Worse, the persistent writer_loop (persistent.rs:1237-1254) does NOT tear down on a write error: a FireForget write failure only `tracing::warn!`s and a WithAck failure is just sent back over the oneshot, then the loop pulls the NEXT OutboundFrame and writes it onto the same socket — directly after the truncated frame. So a single 2s write timeout (DEFAULT_WRITE_TIMEOUT) under backpressure corrupts the stream for the device with no recovery, and unlike the read path this is not even classified as fatal. Note: the timeout here is intentionally encoded as IOError(TimedOut) (not ReadTimeout), which is correct for the trait contract (that contract is read-only), but it does not change the desync.
confirmed.suggestedFix: A partially-written ADB frame is unrecoverable for the framed peer, so a write timeout must be treated as fatal to the connection, not a per-frame soft error. Two parts: (1) in the transport, once any bytes of a frame have been written, a subsequent timeout should poison the connection (e.g. shut down the write half / mark it dead) rather than returning a recoverable-looking error that lets the next frame be appended to the truncation; (2) in persistent.rs::writer_loop, a write failure on the shared socket should break the loop and tear the connection down (matching how the reader treats fatal errors), since after a partial write the stream alignment with the device is gone. Alternatively, only apply the timeout at frame boundaries (write each frame with no mid-frame cancellation) and rely on TCP/socket-level write timeouts.
confirmed.verifierReasoning:
Verified against the actual code; all cited facts hold.

(1) tcp_transport.rs:122-141 — write_all_timeout wraps `writer.write_all(data)` + `flush()` in tokio::time::timeout. AsyncWriteExt::write_all is NOT cancel-safe: it advances an internal cursor across repeated poll_write calls, each handing bytes to the kernel socket send buffer. When the timeout fires and drops the future mid-flush, the already-flushed prefix has been delivered to the peer (adbd) and cannot be recalled; the unwritten tail is simply abandoned. Result: a truncated ADB frame on the wire. This is the exact write-side analog of the verified read_exact desync.

(2) write_message_with_timeout (lines 290-308) calls write_all_timeout twice — header (24B) then payload — so the timeout can split the 24-byte header itself, or land between header and payload, or mid-payload. Any of these leaves a partial frame.

(3) writer_loop (persistent.rs:1237-1256) confirmed: FireForget write error only `tracing::warn!`s; WithAck sends the error over the oneshot. Neither breaks the loop or tears down the connection. The loop immediately recv()s the next OutboundFrame and writes it onto the SAME socket, appended directly after the truncation -> permanent host->device frame desync.

(4) DEFAULT_WRITE_TIMEOUT = 2s (adb_message_transport.rs:10), used by write_message which the writer_loop calls. The timeout is reachable under genuine TCP send-buffer backpressure (full kernel buffer / slow or stalled peer), so write_all can exceed 2s — not theoretical.

(5) USB immunity confirmed: usb_transport.rs:246-267 transfer_with_timeout does an atomic cancel_all() of the pending bulk transfer on timeout and surfaces Cancelled -> ReadTimeout; a cancelled URB does not deliver a partial bulk transfer into the device's framing. So the finding's "write-side sibling / USB has a guarantee TCP lacks" framing is accurate.

Attempted refutation (partial mitigation, but does NOT refute): on the WithAck path, poll_inflight_write (persistent.rs:2254-2257) calls shared.mark_closed() on a write error. But mark_closed is a per-SessionInner atomic flag (persistent.rs:1834), failing only the one session that issued the timed-out WRTE. It does NOT tear down the shared connection: the writer_loop and socket survive, and (a) other live sessions and (b) ALL subsequent FireForget control frames (OKAY/CLSE/OPEN/raw) continue writing onto the corrupted stream. The FireForget path has zero mitigation (warn-and-continue). So the connection-wide host->device desync genuinely holds, with no recovery.

The finding's note that the IOError(TimedOut) encoding is fine for the (read-only) timeout trait contract is correct and not the defect. The defect is partial-write-then-continue. High severity is appropriate: a single 2s write timeout under backpressure corrupts the device-bound stream for every session on the connection, and unlike the read desync it is never classified as fatal. The suggested fix (treat a mid-frame write timeout as connection-fatal / break the writer_loop and tear down, or apply timeouts only at frame boundaries) is the correct direction and matches the established meta-pattern of giving the TCP path the robustness the USB path already has.

confirmed.title: TCP read_exact_timeout is not cancel-safe: a 1s reader-loop timeout crossing a partial header/payload read drops already-read bytes and permanently desyncs the framed stream
confirmed.scenario: This IS the reference bug, verified against the actual call path. read_exact_timeout does `tokio::time::timeout(timeout, reader.read_exact(buf))`. AsyncReadExt::read_exact is NOT cancel-safe: when the timeout elapses, the timeout future is dropped, which drops the read_exact future, and any bytes it had already moved from the socket into `buf` are lost (read_exact buffers internally / has consumed them from the kernel). read_message_with_timeout (lines 244-288) calls it twice with the SAME timeout passed from the persistent reader loop: once for the 24-byte header (line 253) and once for the data_length payload (line 269). The reader loop calls read_message_with_timeout(Duration::from_secs(1)) (persistent.rs:1176). Failure path: the header read completes, the device then sends a large WRTE payload that arrives in fragments; the 1s deadline fires after, say, 4000 of 8192 payload bytes have been pulled off the socket into msg_data. The future is dropped, those 4000 bytes are gone, and read_message_with_timeout returns Err(ReadTimeout). The reader loop classifies ReadTimeout as a benign idle timeout (persistent.rs:1013, ReadStep::ReadTimeout => continue) and loops. The NEXT read_message_with_timeout reads its 24-byte 'header' starting at payload byte 4000 — mid-payload garbage. Best case the command word is unknown -> ADBTransportMessageHeader::try_from -> RustADBError::ConversionError, which the reader loop treats as FATAL (persistent.rs:1029-1044, only InvalidIntegrity is recoverable) -> reader breaks -> connection torn down, every multiplexed session dies. Worse case the garbage decodes to a plausible header with a huge data_length, mis-framing all subsequent traffic. USB is immune because usb_transport keeps read_residual across calls AND its timeout is nusb's atomic transfer cancellation (transfer_with_timeout, usb_transport.rs:246-267) — no half-frame is ever left consumed-but-lost.
confirmed.suggestedFix: Give the TCP read path the same cross-call durability the USB path has. Either (a) keep a per-connection residual/partial buffer so a timed-out read_exact preserves the bytes already read and resumes from them on the next call (mirroring usb_transport's read_residual + fill_and_carry), or (b) only apply the idle timeout to the FIRST byte of a frame and, once any frame byte has been consumed, switch to an un-timed (or much longer, disconnect-only) read_exact so a frame is always read atomically to completion — never returning ReadTimeout after partial consumption. Option (b) matches the trait contract intent: ReadTimeout must mean 'no partial message consumed'. The reader loop's own doc (persistent.rs:984-996) already states a frame read must be atomic; the TCP impl is the one transport that breaks it.
confirmed.verifierReasoning:
Verified against the actual code on all load-bearing claims.

(1) tcp_transport.rs:108-120 — read_exact_timeout is exactly as quoted: tokio::time::timeout(timeout, reader.read_exact(buf)). tokio's AsyncReadExt::read_exact is documented as NOT cancel-safe; when the timeout future fires it drops the read_exact future and the bytes already drained from the kernel into the local buf are lost (buf is call-scoped and discarded on the Err path). No residual/carry buffer exists on the TCP side to preserve them.

(2) read_message_with_timeout (tcp_transport.rs:244-288) calls read_exact_timeout twice with the same read_timeout: line 253 for the 24-byte header, line 269 for the data_length payload (payload length already bounded by payload_len_within_bound, so allocation abuse is separately guarded, but that does not affect the partial-read desync).

(3) persistent.rs:1176 confirms the reader loop calls read_message_with_timeout(Duration::from_secs(1)). persistent.rs:1013/1197 confirm ReadStep::ReadTimeout => continue (benign idle). persistent.rs:1039 confirms ONLY RustADBError::InvalidIntegrity is recoverable; ConversionError (raised by ADBTransportMessageHeader::try_from before payload length is known) and the oversize-bound ADBRequestFailed are explicitly fatal -> break -> connection teardown killing all multiplexed sessions. The loop's own doc (984-996) states a frame read must be atomic and that dropping it mid-frame desyncs the stream.

(4) Failure path is concrete: header read completes, payload read of N bytes times out after pulling some-but-not-all payload bytes off the socket; those bytes are lost; ReadTimeout returned; loop continues; next read_message_with_timeout reads its 24-byte header starting mid-payload -> almost certainly an unknown command word -> ConversionError -> fatal teardown (or, worse, a plausible header with a large data_length mis-framing all subsequent traffic).

(5) USB asymmetry confirmed: usb_transport.rs holds read_residual: Vec<u8> (line 66) carried across calls; read_exact (471) drains residual first and fill_and_carry (515) stashes over-read; transfer_with_timeout (246-267) uses nusb's atomic cancel_all + next_complete drain and maps Cancelled->ReadTimeout (282), so a timeout never leaves a partially-consumed-and-lost frame field. This is precisely the cross-call durability the TCP path lacks.

The finding is the verified reference root-cause bug, correctly located and correctly explained. Severity critical is justified: one idle-timeout crossing a partial payload permanently desyncs the stream and tears down every multiplexed session over that TCP connection.

confirmed.title: TCP read holds the read-half lock across two non-cancel-safe read_exact calls; a timeout mid-frame discards already-read bytes and desyncs the stream (no read_residual like USB)
confirmed.scenario: reader_loop calls read_message_with_timeout(1s). Inside, the read_half lock is held while read_exact_timeout runs twice: once for the 24-byte header (line 253) and again for the payload (line 269). read_exact_timeout wraps reader.read_exact in tokio::time::timeout (line 113); AsyncReadExt::read_exact is NOT cancel-safe, so when the 1s deadline fires after part of the payload has been read into msg_data, the future is dropped and those bytes are LOST. Unlike USBTransport (which carries over-read bytes in Connection::read_residual across calls, and whose timeout is nusb's atomic transfer cancellation), TcpTransport keeps no residual: the next reader iteration re-locks read_half and starts a fresh read_exact from the MIDDLE of the old payload. The next 24 bytes are payload bytes, the header decode then sees an illegal command word -> RustADBError::ConversionError -> classify_read_result -> ReadStep::ReadError -> reader_loop treats ConversionError as FATAL (persistent.rs:1029-1044) and tears the whole multiplexed connection down. This is the verified reference bug; the lock dimension is that the loss happens while the read-half lock is held, and the per-field timeout (below) makes a slow-but-live payload trip it, not just an idle link.
confirmed.suggestedFix: Give TcpTransport the same robustness guarantee USBTransport already has: keep a persistent read buffer/residual on the transport and read into it incrementally with a cancel-safe primitive (e.g. accumulate via poll_read / a manual loop over read() that retains partial bytes across timeouts), so a timeout never discards consumed bytes. The framed stream then stays aligned exactly as the USB read_residual path does, and ReadTimeout only ever fires on a clean frame boundary.

A timeout firing mid-payload therefore discards consumed payload bytes. (3) TcpTransport carries NO residual buffer — grep confirms read_residual exists only in usb_transport.rs:66 (carried across read_exact calls at lines 403/422). So the next reader iteration re-locks read_half and starts a fresh read_exact from the middle of the abandoned payload. (4) Those mid-payload bytes are decoded as a header: ADBTransportMessageHeader::try_from -> MessageCommand::try_from(...).map_err(|_| RustADBError::ConversionError) at adb_transport_message.rs:130-131 yields ConversionError on an illegal command word. The full failure chain holds exactly as described and is the same class as the verified reference bug. The real defect is the lost-bytes desync from a non-cancel-safe read with no residual, which is precisely what the scenario and suggested fix target. This does not change isReal or severity.

confirmed.title: USB read_exact loses partially-read frame bytes on a mid-frame timeout, then returns the benign ReadTimeout (continue) -> stream desync
confirmed.scenario: read_message_with_timeout reads each frame field (24-byte header at line 403, then data_length payload at 420) via read_exact, which LOOPS over transfer_with_timeout (line 492) because a field can span multiple max_packet_size-aligned bulk IN transfers. If transfer N succeeds (copy_len bytes written into `out`, offset advanced) but a LATER transfer in the same field times out, transfer_with_timeout returns TransferError::Cancelled, map_transfer_status (line 493) turns it into RustADBError::ReadTimeout, and `?` propagates it out of read_exact / read_message_with_timeout. The bytes already copied into the local `out` buffer are dropped on the floor (out is a stack/heap-local of this call), while the device has already put those bytes on the wire. classify_read_result maps ReadTimeout -> ReadStep::ReadTimeout, and reader_loop does `continue` (persistent.rs:1013), starting a FRESH 24-byte header read. But the device's next bytes are the *remainder of the timed-out field*, not a header -> the framed stream is desynced exactly like the known TCP read_exact_timeout bug. The summary claims USB is immune because nusb's cancellation is atomic per transfer; that is true for ONE transfer, but read_exact issues multiple transfers per frame field and only the residual over-read is preserved across calls -- bytes consumed INTO `out` by completed earlier transfers of the same field are not. The 1s reader-loop timeout makes a mid-multi-transfer deadline genuinely reachable for any payload larger than one aligned transfer under throughput stalls.
confirmed.suggestedFix: Make read_exact frame-atomic against a mid-field timeout the same way over-read is carried: on a ReadTimeout after offset>0, stash the partially-filled `out[..offset]` into a per-connection 'partial frame field' carry (or treat any in-progress field as residual) so the next call resumes instead of restarting a header read. Equivalently, only honor the timeout at a frame boundary (offset==0 with empty residual); once any byte of a frame has been consumed, keep reading to field completion (ignoring the per-read deadline) so a ReadTimeout is never returned mid-frame. This matches the trait contract intent ('timeout before a COMPLETE message') and restores the residual-preserving guarantee the USB path is assumed to have.
confirmed.verifierReasoning:
Verified against the actual code in usb_transport.rs (read_exact at lines 471-509, transfer_with_timeout at 246-267, map_transfer_status at 279-285) and persistent.rs (reader loop at 1005-1044).

The failure path holds and is structurally the same class as the verified TCP read_exact_timeout bug:

1) read_exact loops while offset < out.len() (line 488). Each iteration requests request_len = aligned_request_len(remaining) and awaits one transfer. A bulk IN transfer ends early on a short packet (documented at line 451 and proven reachable by the test fill_and_carry_short_packet_partial_fill at lines 630-640, whose own comment says 'the caller loops for the rest'). So a single frame field CAN span multiple transfers, with offset advanced > 0 after a short first transfer and residual left EMPTY (a short packet carries nothing — line 639).
2) If a LATER transfer in the same field times out, transfer_with_timeout returns TransferError::Cancelled (lines 258-265), map_transfer_status turns it into RustADBError::ReadTimeout (line 282), and `?` at line 493 propagates it out of read_exact / read_message_with_timeout (lines 403, 427).
3) The bytes already copied into out[..offset] live in the caller's local `data`/`msg_data` buffer (lines 402, 419) and are dropped on the early return. fill_and_carry only stashes OVER-read overshoot into residual (lines 515-522); it never stashes bytes already written into dst. So the consumed prefix of the field is genuinely lost, while its remainder is still on the wire.
4) classify_read_result maps ReadTimeout -> ReadStep::ReadTimeout (line 1197) and the reader loop does `continue` (line 1013), restarting a fresh 24-byte header read. The next wire bytes are the field remainder, not a header -> permanent framed-stream desync, exactly like the TCP bug.

The summary's 'USB is immune' claim is only valid for a single transfer; read_exact issues multiple transfers per field and only the residual over-read is preserved across the timeout. The reader-loop comment at 1019-1042 carefully reasons about frame-alignment for InvalidIntegrity vs ConversionError but implicitly assumes ReadTimeout is always frame-aligned — which this path violates.

Why medium (not high) confidence/severity: with request_len requesting the entire aligned remaining field in one transfer, a well-behaved device sending a contiguous payload usually completes the field in a single transfer (full length or one terminating short packet), so the multi-transfer-per-field precondition requires a mid-payload short packet followed by a >1s stall. That is genuinely reachable under throughput stalls / packet coalescing on large reverse payloads, but less frequent than the TCP case where header and payload are always two distinct read_exact calls. The bug class, mechanism, and consequence match the finding exactly; the suggested fix (carry partial-field bytes, or only honor the timeout at offset==0 with empty residual) is the correct direction.

confirmed.title: writer_loop never tears down on a persistently failing write half; a half-open transport keeps reporting is_alive()=true while every write silently fails
confirmed.scenario: writer_loop drains the outbound queue forever: a FireForget write error is logged and the loop continues (lines 1241-1243); a WithAck write error is forwarded to that one caller's oneshot but the loop also continues. There is no fatal classification on the write side -- a dead/half-open write endpoint (write direction broken while read still blocks on its 1s idle timeout) causes every OKAY/CLSE/OPEN to be logged-and-dropped and every WRTE to fail per-call, indefinitely, with no teardown and no signal to the reader. is_alive() only consults reader_handle (lines 1698-1703), so the connection reports alive while writes are uniformly failing. Flow-control deadlock is also possible: if OKAY credit grants cannot be written out, the peer stalls, the reader sees only idle ReadTimeouts (continue), and nothing ever breaks. Contrast the reader, which correctly breaks on a fatal read error.
confirmed.suggestedFix: Classify write errors like the reader does: distinguish a transport-fatal write failure (IOError BrokenPipe/NotConnected, nusb transfer error other than a timeout) from a transient one. On a fatal write error, signal teardown -- e.g. set conn_closed and drop the writer (so subsequent enqueues fail fast with BrokenPipe) and/or abort the reader -- instead of looping forever. At minimum, have is_alive() also reflect writer_handle.is_finished() so a dead writer is observable.
confirmed.verifierReasoning: Verified against actual code. writer_loop at persistent.rs:1238-1255 matches the quoted evidence exactly and indeed has no fatal-error branch and no break -- it loops until all senders drop. is_alive() at 1698-1703 only checks reader_handle. The reader's fatal/recoverable split (1018-1044) breaks on fatal read errors, but a half-open write half produces NO read error -- reads just hit idle ReadTimeout and continue (1013), so the reader's correct teardown never triggers. The inbound-crediting OKAY is enqueued as FireForget (2200) and would be logged-and-dropped on a failed write, which is a genuine flow-control stall path with no teardown. is_alive() gates connection reuse in default_backend.rs (213, 222, 358), so a half-open connection is reused as alive -- the observable harm the finding claims. REFUTATION of one sub-claim: the WRTE data path is not silent. poll_inflight_write (2254-2257) surfaces the WithAck write error to the application as an io::Error and calls shared.mark_closed(), so application writes fail loudly and the session is retired. The finding's strongest wording ("every WRTE fails per-call indefinitely with no signal") is therefore inaccurate, but the underlying structural bug (no writer-side teardown, is_alive ignores writer, silent FireForget credit loss enabling a half-open stall) is real. Medium severity is appropriate.
confirmed.verifierCorrection: The structural defect is real but the finding's "every WRTE silently fails with no signal" framing is partly wrong. WRTE writes are NOT silent: a WithAck write error is returned over the oneshot and surfaced to the application by poll_inflight_write (persistent.rs:2254-2257 -> Poll::Ready(Err(e))), which ALSO calls shared.mark_closed() so that session fails loud and subsequent poll_read/poll_write get BrokenPipe. The accurate residual bug is narrower: (1) writer_loop (persistent.rs:1238-1255) has no fatal classification or teardown for FireForget frames -- OKAY/CLSE/OPEN write errors are logged-and-dropped and the loop continues indefinitely; (2) is_alive() (persistent.rs:1698-1703) consults only reader_handle, never writer_handle; (3) the inbound flow-control crediting OKAY is FireForget (persistent.rs:2200), so on a half-open write half those credits are silently lost. Net effect on a half-open TCP transport (write direction broken, read direction only idling): the reader never errors (it sees only ReadTimeout -> continue at persistent.rs:1013), the peer stalls for lack of inbound credit, the connection reports is_alive()=true, and default_backend.rs (213/222/358) keeps handing it out for reuse. So the connection-level "no teardown / reports alive while the write half is dead" claim and the flow-control-deadlock scenario hold; the per-WRTE "silent failure" claim does not.

confirmed.title: TCP read_message_with_timeout returns neutral ReadTimeout AFTER consuming a partial frame (header read, payload-phase timeout) — violates the contract's "before a complete message" premise and desyncs the stream
confirmed.scenario: The trait contract (adb_message_transport.rs:37-46) says implementations MUST return RustADBError::ReadTimeout when the timeout elapses BEFORE a complete message. The intent is that the persistent reader (classify_read_result -> ReadStep::ReadTimeout -> `continue`, persistent.rs:1194-1200, 1013) can safely keep looping because nothing was consumed. TcpTransport::read_message_with_timeout applies the SAME `read_timeout` independently to two separate read_exact_timeout calls: the 24-byte header (line 253) and then the payload (line 269). Concrete failure: the header read completes within the window, then the payload read (e.g. device pauses mid-frame, or large payload) hits the 1s deadline at line 269 -> read_exact_timeout returns Err(RustADBError::ReadTimeout) (line 118). The reader loop sees ReadTimeout and `continue`s as if nothing happened — but the header has already been consumed off the socket while the payload bytes are still pending on the wire. The next loop iteration's header read (line 253) reads the leftover payload bytes as a 24-byte header -> ConversionError (illegal command word), which classify_read_result/the reader loop treat as FATAL (payload not proven frame-aligned, persistent.rs:1029-1038) -> connection torn down. So although the error mapping to ReadTimeout is technically correct, returning it mid-frame breaks the safety guarantee the neutral signal is supposed to carry. This is the timeout-contract face of the verified reference TCP cancel-safety/desync bug (read_exact dropping partial bytes); here the partial-consume happens at the header/payload field boundary rather than within one read_exact. USB does not split the timeout window this way into a fatal outcome because its read_residual carries over-read bytes across calls, but the TCP path has no residual buffer.
confirmed.suggestedFix: Apply the timeout as a single deadline across the WHOLE message (header + payload), not per read_exact call, and only return ReadTimeout when it fires before any byte of the frame is consumed. Concretely: compute a deadline = Instant::now() + read_timeout once, wrap the combined header+payload read in one tokio::time::timeout_at(deadline, ...); if the timeout fires after the header was partially/fully read, that is NOT a clean idle timeout — either buffer the partial bytes across calls (a TCP read_residual mirroring USB) so the next read resumes mid-frame, or classify a mid-frame timeout as a fatal/desync error rather than the benign ReadTimeout. The neutral ReadTimeout must only be returned when zero bytes of the current frame have been consumed.
confirmed.verifierReasoning: Verified against actual code. tcp_transport.rs:252-253 reads the fixed 24-byte header via a first read_exact_timeout (fully consuming 24 bytes off the socket), then lines 267-269 read the payload via a SECOND, independent read_exact_timeout using the SAME read_timeout. read_exact_timeout (lines 113-118) returns RustADBError::ReadTimeout on elapse. So a payload-phase timeout returns the transport-neutral ReadTimeout AFTER the header has already been consumed and committed, while the payload bytes are still pending on the wire. This violates the contract premise in adb_message_transport.rs:39-46, which scopes ReadTimeout to "before a COMPLETE message" precisely so the persistent reader can treat it as a no-op idle timeout. The reader loop confirms this assumption: read_or_control passes Duration::from_secs(1) (persistent.rs:1176), classify_read_result maps ReadTimeout to ReadStep::ReadTimeout (1197), and the loop does `continue` (1013) without compensating for the consumed header. On the next iteration the leftover payload bytes are read as a 24-byte header; an unknown command word yields ConversionError (adb_transport_message.rs:126/130-131), which the loop classifies as FATAL (persistent.rs:1039-1044, since it is not InvalidIntegrity) and tears down the connection. The TCP/USB contrast is also confirmed: grep shows TCP has no residual buffer, while USB carries over-read bytes in read_residual and uses atomic per-transfer nusb cancellation (usb_transport.rs:471-508), so a USB mid-frame timeout does not desync. This is genuinely the timeout-contract face of the reference cancel-safety/desync bug, occurring at the header/payload field boundary rather than within a single read_exact. The failure path concretely holds; it is reachable whenever the payload arrives in a later TCP segment that crosses the 1s deadline (slow/paused device, large or fragmented payload). I set severity to high rather than critical because the trigger requires the timeout to land specifically in the payload phase after a successful header read — header+payload are usually written contiguously — so while structurally certain and reachable on the production 1s reader path, it is less frequent than an unconditional break. Suggested fix is sound: a single deadline across the whole frame plus either a TCP residual buffer mirroring USB or classifying a mid-frame timeout as fatal/desync rather than the benign ReadTimeout; the neutral ReadTimeout must only be returned when zero bytes of the current frame have been consumed.

confirmed.title: recv_file indexes payload[len-8..len-4] without a length guard → remote-triggerable panic on a short device frame
confirmed.scenario: recv_file is the sync-pull drain reached via pull() over the core ADBMessageTransport (both USB adb_usb_device.rs:144 and TCP adb_tcp_device.rs:65 → commands/pull.rs:61). On every loop iteration it unconditionally slices the DONE-trailer out of the raw device payload: `payload[(payload.len() - 8)..(payload.len() - 4)]`. `payload` is exactly the bytes a device WRTE frame delivered (transport already accepts any data_length from 0..=MAX_PAYLOAD). A device (hostile, or simply buggy/at a chunk boundary) that sends a WRTE whose payload is shorter than 8 bytes — including an empty payload — makes `payload.len() - 8` underflow in usize (wraps to ~1.8e19) and the slice index goes out of bounds, panicking the task. With an empty payload the inner `while rdr.position() != payload.len()` loop at line 88 never runs and execution falls straight through to this slice, so 0-byte and 1..=7-byte payloads both panic. This is a remote-controlled panic on the wire path; unlike the integrity/bound checks the other read paths perform, there is no `if payload.len() >= 8` guard here.
confirmed.suggestedFix: Guard the length before slicing: `if payload.len() < 8 { return Err(RustADBError::ConversionError); }` (or treat a short trailer as 'not DONE, keep looping'). Use checked subtraction / `payload.get(payload.len()-8..payload.len()-4)` and map None to a structured error so a short/empty device frame cannot panic the process.
confirmed.verifierReasoning:
Verified against the actual code. adb_session.rs:113-115 unconditionally slices `payload[(payload.len() - 8)..(payload.len() - 4)]` with no length guard. `payload` is the raw device frame from `recv_and_reply_okay().into_payload()` (line 83). The frame's data_length is only upper-bounded: adb_transport_message.rs:44 documents `data_length: u32, /* length of payload (0 is allowed) */`, and tcp_transport.rs:257-277 / payload_len_within_bound only reject data_length > MAX_PAYLOAD, constructing an empty Vec when data_length == 0 (line 267 `if header.data_length() != 0`). No lower-bound or is_empty check exists on the read path. The call path is real: pull() in adb_usb_device.rs:144 and adb_tcp_device.rs:65 → commands/pull.rs:61 → recv_file.

For a 0-byte payload the inner `while rdr.position() != payload.len()` loop at line 88 is skipped (0 != 0 is false), so execution falls straight through to line 113 where `payload.len() - 8` = `0usize - 8` underflows (wraps to ~1.8e19) and the slice index goes out of bounds, panicking the task. This is remote-triggerable by a hostile or buggy device sending an empty WRTE frame.

One correction to the finding's wording: the claim that 1..=7-byte payloads also panic is overstated. For nonempty short payloads the inner loop runs, takes the `Some(0)|None` branch, does `seek_relative(4)` (Cursor seek does not bounds-check) then `read_u32`, which returns an EOF error via `?` (early return, not panic) when fewer than 4 bytes follow. So short-nonempty frames most likely error out rather than panic. The guaranteed panic is the empty (0-byte) payload, which is itself a fully valid frame per the documented contract. This nuance does not weaken the core bug. Severity high is appropriate: a single 0-byte WRTE on the wire path panics the task; the fix is a length guard / checked subtraction (payload.get(...)) before the slice. Distinct class from the TCP timeout cancel-safety bug, consistent with sameClassAsTcpBug:false.
confirmed.verifierCorrection: The 0-byte (empty) payload case is a guaranteed panic at adb_session.rs:114 via usize underflow in `payload.len() - 8`. The finding's secondary claim that 1..=7-byte payloads also panic is inaccurate: those nonempty short frames most likely return a structured EOF error from `read_u32`'s `?` inside the inner loop (Cursor::seek_relative does not bounds-check, but read_u32 errors on insufficient bytes) before reaching line 113, rather than panicking. The real, confirmed remote-triggerable panic is the empty-payload path. Fix: guard with `if payload.len() < 8 { return Err(...) }` or use `payload.get(payload.len()-8..payload.len()-4)` / checked_sub before slicing.

confirmed.title: Proxy framebuffer allocates vec![0u8; framebuffer_info.size] from an unbounded device u32 (no payload_len_within_bound analogue)
confirmed.scenario: framebuffer_inner reads the FrameBufferInfoV1/V2 struct straight off the connection and then does `vec![0u8; framebuffer_info.size as usize]` where `size` is an attacker/device-controlled u32 (up to ~4 GiB). Unlike the two message-transport read paths (tcp_transport.rs:260 / usb_transport.rs:411) which gate every payload allocation behind `payload_len_within_bound(MAX_PAYLOAD)`, this single-shot allocation has no upper bound — only a `try_into()` that fails on 32-bit usize but succeeds on 64-bit. A malicious/garbled framebuffer header drives one immediate multi-GiB allocation (OOM / abort) before any data is read. The message-device equivalent (commands/framebuffer.rs) avoids this by draining into a growing Vec frame-by-frame instead of pre-allocating, so this is specifically the proxy path missing the bound the rest of the codebase already standardized on.
confirmed.suggestedFix: Bound `framebuffer_info.size` against a sane maximum (e.g. width*height*4 computed with checked_mul, or a fixed cap) before allocating, mirroring payload_len_within_bound; reject oversize with ADBRequestFailed instead of allocating blindly.
confirmed.verifierReasoning:
Verified against actual code. adboost/src/proxy/device_commands/framebuffer.rs lines 33-43 (V1) and 63-73 (V2) do `vec![0u8; framebuffer_info.size.try_into().map_err(...)?]`. framebuffer_info.size is a u32 (models/framebuffer_info.rs:18,60) decoded directly off the connection via LittleEndian::read_u32 with zero validation. On 64-bit targets usize is u64, so u32->usize try_into always succeeds; the try_into is effectively a no-op guard (it can only fail if size > usize::MAX, impossible for a u32). So a garbled/malicious framebuffer header drives one immediate allocation up to ~4 GiB before any pixel data is read — a DoS/OOM-abort vector, reachable in the proxy passthrough path where the peer device controls the bytes.

The finding's two contrast claims both check out: (1) the message-transport read paths gate every payload allocation behind payload_len_within_bound(MAX_PAYLOAD) at tcp_transport.rs:260 and usb_transport.rs:411; (2) the message-device equivalent (message_devices/commands/framebuffer.rs:34-44/67-77) grows a Vec frame-by-frame with read_to_end + extend_from_slice rather than pre-allocating from size. So this is genuinely the proxy path missing the bound the rest of the codebase standardized on — the same meta-pattern as the reference TCP bug (a non-transport/async path missing a robustness guarantee present elsewhere), though a different bug class (unbounded alloc, not cancel-safety/desync).

Severity medium is appropriate, not higher: it is a single bounded-by-u32 allocation, not a panic or memory-safety issue — Vec zero-init of ~4 GiB usually succeeds via lazy zero pages or aborts on alloc failure rather than corrupting state, and the value originates from the connected (potentially trusted) device. The suggested fix (bound size against width*height*4 via checked_mul, or a fixed cap, rejecting oversize) is sound.

confirmed.title: Proxy LIST/RECV allocate vec![0u8; len] from an unbounded LE u32 read off the wire
confirmed.scenario: In the LIST (DENT) path, `name_len = connection.read_u32_le().await?` is a raw device-supplied u32 and is used directly as `vec![0_u8; name_len as usize]` with no upper bound. The same pattern exists in recv.rs:62-63 (`let length = connection.read_u32_le().await? as usize; let mut error_msg = vec![0; length];`) for a FAIL reason. A malicious or corrupt device response can request up to ~4 GiB per entry. Lower severity than the transport path because it is the proxy-to-adb-server channel and the subsequent read_exact will fail/EOF, but the allocation happens before the read, so it is still an alloc-from-wire DoS without the MAX_PAYLOAD-style guard the message transports enforce.
confirmed.suggestedFix: Clamp these wire lengths to a reasonable maximum (filename/error-string sized, e.g. a few KiB, or at most MAX_PAYLOAD) before allocating, or read incrementally into a bounded buffer rather than pre-sizing from the untrusted length.
confirmed.verifierReasoning:
The cited code is exact. In adboost/src/proxy/device_commands/list.rs, the DENT branch reads `let name_len = connection.read_u32_le().await?;` then `let mut name_buf = vec![0_u8; name_len as usize];` then `connection.read_exact(&mut name_buf).await?;` (the loop at lines ~53-79). `name_len` is a raw, device-supplied little-endian u32 with no upper bound, used directly to size a zeroed allocation BEFORE any read. The same pattern exists in recv.rs FAIL branch: `let length = connection.read_u32_le().await? as usize; let mut error_msg = vec![0; length];` then read_exact. (The recv.rs DATA branch is safe — it reads in BUFFER_SIZE=65535 chunks via `chunk`, not a single sized alloc.)

This is a genuine alloc-from-wire pattern: a compromised/buggy device's sync reply can specify up to u32::MAX (~4 GiB) and force the proxy to allocate+zero that much before the subsequent read_exact fails/EOFs. The message-transport layer deliberately guards this exact risk with `payload_len_within_bound`/MAX_PAYLOAD (adb_transport_message.rs:19/29, enforced at tcp_transport.rs:258 and usb_transport.rs:409 which reject data_length > MAX_PAYLOAD before reading the payload) — the sync proxy commands have no equivalent clamp. So the finding's core claim (missing the MAX_PAYLOAD-style guard) is correct.

Severity is correctly self-assessed as low and confirmed: (1) the connection is the proxy→local-adb-server TcpStream (default 127.0.0.1:5037), so the threat actor is a malicious/compromised device relayed by the local adb server, not arbitrary remote input; (2) `vec![0u8; n]` aborts on allocation failure rather than panicking, and a large-but-succeeding alloc causes transient memory pressure rather than a guaranteed crash; (3) it is a single allocation per response branch, and the following read_exact will error/EOF, ending the loop. It is correctly flagged as NOT the same class as the TCP read_exact cancel-safety desync bug. Real but low-severity defensive gap.
